title: Hissing under the hood
h1: Why is there a hissing noise under my hood?
metaDesc: Hissing from under the hood? Answer a few quick questions to see if it's a coolant leak, vacuum leak or something normal, how urgent it is, and what to do next.
synonyms: hissing when I press the brake
intro: A hiss from under the hood is air, steam or gas escaping somewhere. Sometimes it's harmless, like the cooling system settling after you park. Other times it's a coolant leak about to cause overheating. A few questions can help you narrow down which, and how quickly to act.
safety: If you see steam or the temperature gauge is in the red, pull over and turn the engine off.
Never open the radiator or coolant cap on a hot engine. Hot coolant can spray out and burn you.
If you smell raw fuel, pull over as soon as it's safe and turn the engine off, keep flames and sparks away, and don't restart it.
If you see smoke or smell burning, pull over as soon as it's safe, turn the engine off and step away from the car.

q_danger.q: Along with the hissing, do you notice any of these?
q_danger.help: Steam looks like white vapor that disappears quickly in the air. Coolant often smells sweet, like syrup.

opts.a: Steam from under the hood, or the temperature gauge is high or in the red
A strong smell of raw fuel
Smoke or a burning smell
None of these
I'm not sure

q_check_gauge.q: With the car safely parked, look at the temperature gauge and under the hood. What do you see?
q_check_gauge.help: Look, but don't open the radiator or coolant cap while the engine is hot.

opts.a: The gauge is high or a temperature warning light is on
The gauge is normal and there's no steam, smoke or fuel smell
I'm not sure, or I can't tell

q_when.q: When do you hear the hiss?

opts.a: While the engine is running, most of the time
Only when I press or release the brake pedal
After I turn the engine off, for a minute or two
When the A/C is on, or right after I switch it off
I'm not sure

q_running.q: While it's hissing, does anything else seem off?
q_running.help: A "rough idle" means the engine shakes or the speed bounces up and down while you're stopped.

opts.a: Rough idle, stalling, or the check engine light is on
The coolant level keeps dropping, or there's a sweet smell
The engine runs normally. It's just the hiss
I'm not sure

q_after_off.q: After you turn the engine off, which fits best?

opts.a: A soft hiss that fades within a minute or two. The gauge was normal and there's no smell or drips
A sweet smell, drips under the front, or a low coolant reservoir
Bubbling or gurgling from the coolant reservoir after a hot drive
I'm not sure

result.title: The engine may be overheating, with coolant escaping as steam
result.now: Pull over somewhere safe, turn the engine off and let it cool for at least 30 minutes. Don't open the coolant cap. Plan on a tow or a mechanic who comes to you.
if: If the gauge went into the red, don't restart it even after adding coolant. Running an overheated engine can warp or crack expensive parts.
If the gauge only rose a little and the engine is now cool, you can check the coolant level in the reservoir, but still have the leak found before relying on the car.
If the oil pressure light comes on or the engine knocks, pull over as soon as it's safe, turn it off and don't restart it.
result.why: Hissing with steam or a high temperature reading means coolant is boiling or spraying out under pressure. Without enough coolant the engine heats up fast, and driving further risks serious engine damage.

causes.name: Leaking or burst coolant hose
causes.clues: Steam or coolant spray from one spot, a wet or swollen hose, or a puddle under the front.

causes.name: Leaking radiator or radiator cap
causes.clues: Crusty green, orange or pink residue around the radiator or cap.

causes.name: Failed cooling fan, water pump or thermostat
causes.clues: It overheats mostly in traffic (fan), or there's a drip near the front of the engine (water pump).
causes.against: These cause overheating, but the hiss itself usually comes from coolant escaping somewhere.

you: Once the engine is fully cool, check the coolant reservoir level.
Look for wet spots or residue on hoses and the radiator.
shop: Head gasket check if it overheated badly

result.title: A fuel leak is possible. Treat it as a fire risk
result.now: If you're driving, pull over when it's safe. Turn the engine off, get everyone out, and keep sparks, flames and cigarettes away. Don't restart it. Have it towed.
if: If you see fuel dripping or pooling, move well away from the car and call for help.
If the smell fades quickly and there's no wet spot, it still needs to be checked before you drive it.
result.why: Fuel lines on modern engines carry fuel under pressure, so a small crack can hiss or spray. Fuel near a hot engine can catch fire, which is why this is a do-not-drive situation.

causes.name: Leaking fuel line or fitting
causes.clues: A wet spot or drip near the engine or under the car, with a strong gas smell.

causes.name: Leaking fuel injector seal or fuel rail
causes.clues: The smell is strongest at the top of the engine.

causes.name: Evaporative (EVAP) system leak
causes.clues: A faint fuel smell with no drips, sometimes with a check engine light.
causes.against: An EVAP leak usually doesn't hiss loudly or drip.

result.title: Fluid may be leaking onto hot engine or exhaust parts
result.now: If you're driving, pull over when it's safe. Turn the engine off and step away until the smoke stops. Don't restart it. Have it towed or have a mechanic look at it where it's parked.
if: If you see smoke or flames, get everyone away from the car and call 911.
If the smoke stops quickly and you can see a small oil seep, it still needs to be checked before you drive it again.
result.why: A hiss with smoke or a burning smell usually means oil, coolant or another fluid is dripping onto the hot exhaust and boiling off. That can start a fire, and it means the engine is losing fluid it needs.

causes.name: Oil leak onto the exhaust
causes.clues: Blue-gray smoke and a burnt oil smell, often after an oil change or from a leaking valve cover gasket.

causes.name: Coolant leak onto hot parts
causes.clues: White, sweet-smelling vapor.

causes.name: Power steering or transmission fluid leak
causes.clues: A drip near the front, with low fluid in one of those reservoirs.

you: Once cool, check the oil and coolant levels.
Note the color of the smoke.
shop: Leak inspection with the engine running

result.title: The brake assist may have an air leak (brake booster or its vacuum hose)
result.now: Braking may take much more force than usual. If you're on the road, press the pedal firmly, leave plenty of room and pull over when it's safe. Have the brakes checked before using the car again, either by a mechanic who comes to you or with a tow.
if: If the pedal sinks toward the floor, feels soft, or the brake warning light comes on, don't drive it at all. That points to a hydraulic problem, not just the booster.
If the engine also idles rough or stalls when you press the brake, the leak may be large. Don't drive it.
If you smell burning or see brake fluid near the pedal or the master cylinder, don't drive it.
result.why: The brake booster uses engine vacuum to make the pedal easy to press. A hiss when you press or release the pedal often means air is leaking into the booster or its hose. If the booster loses its assist, the pedal gets hard and the car takes much longer to stop, and that can happen without warning.

causes.name: Leaking brake booster diaphragm
causes.clues: The hiss is under the dash near the pedal, and the pedal feels firmer than before.

causes.name: Cracked or loose booster vacuum hose or check valve
causes.clues: The hiss is under the hood, near the back of the engine on the driver's side.

causes.name: Worn seal at the master cylinder
causes.clues: Brake fluid residue where the master cylinder meets the booster.

you: Ask the shop to test the brake booster if the pedal feels hard.
Listen near the pedal and under the hood while someone presses the brake.
shop: Vacuum hose and check valve inspection

result.title: Air is likely leaking into the engine through a hose or seal (vacuum leak)
result.now: Get it checked within the next few days. A smoke test at a shop usually finds the leak quickly.
if: If the check engine light starts flashing or the engine shakes badly, stop driving and have it towed.
If it stalls while you're driving, don't keep driving it. Losing power in traffic is dangerous.
If the brake pedal feels harder than usual, stop driving and have it checked. A vacuum leak can also weaken the brake booster.
result.why: The engine draws air through a network of rubber hoses and seals. When one cracks or comes loose, air rushes in with a hiss, and the extra air throws off the fuel mixture. That causes a rough idle, stalling and a check engine light.

causes.name: Cracked or disconnected vacuum hose
causes.clues: The hiss is louder at idle, and you can see an old, cracked or loose rubber hose.

causes.name: Leaking intake gasket or PCV valve and hose
causes.clues: A high or uneven idle, and lean-condition codes on a scan.

causes.name: Cracked air intake duct
causes.clues: A split in the large rubber duct between the air filter box and the engine.

you: With the engine idling, listen carefully around the top of the engine to find where the hiss is loudest. Keep hands and clothing away from belts and the fan.
Look for hoses that are cracked, brittle or popped off.
shop: Code scan and fuel trim readings

result.title: Possibly a small vacuum or air intake leak
result.now: Book a check when convenient, and mention that the hiss is there while the engine runs.
if: If a rough idle, stalling or a check engine light shows up, get it checked within a few days.
If the temperature gauge starts rising or you notice a sweet smell, treat it as a coolant leak and pull over.
If the brake pedal starts feeling harder than usual, stop driving and have it checked.
result.why: A steady hiss with the engine running well often means a small air leak that the engine is still compensating for. These tend to grow over time and can eventually cause rough running or poor fuel economy.

causes.name: Small vacuum hose leak
causes.clues: The hiss is loudest at idle and quieter when you rev the engine.

causes.name: PCV valve or hose
causes.clues: The hiss is near the valve cover on top of the engine.

causes.name: Small exhaust manifold leak
causes.clues: More of a ticking or puffing sound, loudest on a cold start.
causes.against: Exhaust leaks usually tick rather than hiss steadily.

you: Listen around the engine to find where the hiss is loudest, staying clear of moving parts.
Look for loose or cracked rubber hoses.

result.title: Possibly a coolant leak
result.now: When the engine is fully cool, check the coolant reservoir and top it up to the marked level if it's low. Get the leak found within the next few days, and watch the temperature gauge closely until then.
if: If the temperature gauge rises above normal or you see steam, pull over, turn the engine off and don't drive it further.
If you're adding coolant every few days, have it checked right away. A bigger failure may be close.
If you smell coolant inside the car or the windshield fogs with a greasy film, get it checked before driving further.
result.why: The cooling system runs under pressure, so a small crack or loose clamp can let coolant hiss out as it heats up. A slow leak can turn into overheating with little warning.

causes.name: Leaking hose or loose hose clamp
causes.clues: Wet spots or crusty residue on a hose or at its ends.

causes.name: Leaking radiator or radiator cap
causes.clues: Residue on the radiator, or the hiss seems to come from the cap.

causes.name: Leaking water pump
causes.clues: Drips or residue at the front of the engine, near the belts.

you: With the engine cold, check the coolant level in the reservoir.
Look under the front of the car for green, orange or pink drips.

result.title: Possibly the A/C system, which can hiss normally
result.now: Notice whether the A/C still blows cold. A brief hiss from the dash or under the hood right after you switch the A/C off is normal pressure settling.
if: If the A/C is blowing warm or the hiss is constant while it runs, book an A/C check. The refrigerant may be low from a leak.
If the hiss comes with a burning smell or a squeal from the belts, get it checked soon.
result.why: The A/C system holds refrigerant under high pressure. When the compressor cycles or shuts off, the pressure evens out, and you can hear a short hiss. That's normal. A hiss with poor cooling suggests a leak.

causes.name: Normal pressure equalizing
causes.clues: A short hiss after switching the A/C off, and it still cools well.

causes.name: Low refrigerant from a leak
causes.clues: The A/C is gradually getting weaker.
causes.against: If it still blows cold, a leak is less likely.

causes.name: Expansion valve or other A/C component fault
causes.clues: A constant hiss from behind the dash with poor cooling.

you: Feel whether the vents blow cold with the A/C on.
Note whether the hiss happens only briefly after switching the A/C off.

result.title: A short hiss after you park can be normal, but check the coolant
result.now: Next time the engine is fully cool, check that the coolant reservoir is between the marks and look under the front of the car for drips.
if: If the coolant is low or you see drips, have the cooling system checked within a few days.
If the hiss gets louder, lasts longer, or the temperature gauge reads higher than usual, get it checked soon.
If you see steam or smell burning, pull over when it's safe, turn the engine off and step away from the car.
result.why: After you shut the engine off, hot coolant, the exhaust and the A/C system all settle, which can make soft hissing or ticking sounds for a minute or two. If the coolant level holds steady over the next week or so, with no smell or drips, normal settling is the likely explanation. Checking the level is how you tell.

causes.name: Cooling system or A/C settling after shutdown
causes.clues: A soft hiss that fades quickly, a normal gauge, and a steady coolant level.

causes.name: Small coolant leak hitting hot parts
causes.clues: A sweet smell after parking, or the coolant level slowly dropping.
causes.against: If the coolant level stays steady, a leak is unlikely.

causes.name: Weak radiator cap
causes.clues: Coolant in the reservoir overflows or the hiss comes from the cap area.

you: Check the coolant level when the engine is cold, and note it so you can compare in a week.
Look for drips under the front of the car after parking.

result.title: Treat it as a possible coolant leak until it's checked
result.now: Let the engine cool fully, then check the coolant level. Have the car checked within the next few days, and watch the temperature gauge whenever you drive.
if: If you see steam, smoke or the gauge rising, pull over, turn the engine off and don't drive it further.
If you smell fuel, don't start the engine. Have it towed.
result.why: The most common hissing that leads to real damage is coolant escaping, because it can lead to overheating. Checking the coolant level and the gauge helps rule that in or out.

causes.name: Coolant leak
causes.clues: A sweet smell, drips, or a low reservoir.

causes.name: Vacuum leak
causes.clues: The hiss is there while the engine runs, with a rough idle.

causes.name: Normal settling after shutdown
causes.clues: A short hiss after you park, with nothing else wrong.

you: Check the coolant level with the engine cold.
Record a short video with sound of the hiss for the shop.

result.title: Have a shop pinpoint where the hiss is coming from
result.now: Book a check when convenient. Note when the hiss happens and record a short video with sound to show the technician.
if: If you see steam, the temperature gauge rises, or you smell fuel or burning, pull over and turn the engine off.
If the brake pedal starts feeling hard, stop driving and have the brakes checked. If the engine runs rough, get it checked within a few days.
result.why: Hissing can come from the cooling system, a vacuum leak, the brake booster or the A/C. If you can't tell when it happens, a technician can usually track it down with a pressure test and a smoke test.

causes.name: Vacuum leak
causes.clues: Hissing while the engine runs, louder at idle.

causes.name: Coolant leak
causes.clues: A sweet smell or a dropping coolant level.

causes.name: Brake booster leak
causes.clues: Hissing that changes when you press the brake.

you: Check the coolant level with the engine cold.
Notice whether the hiss changes with the brake pedal or the A/C.
